title: Alpha Trader
content: forever. Instead of working my butt off and squirreling away my gains. I worked when I felt like it because I thought I could come in and make money whenever I wanted. I had no sense of urgency. The positive takeaway. Away from my dumb approach in the late 1990s, was that, when a similar moment of outstanding trading opportunity appeared in 2008, I recognized it. I knew it was time to work as hard as humanly possible, because the period of insane volatility and fat pitches was only temporary, the tuition I paid in 1999 paid off with my best year ever in 2008. 2 failing to ride the ebonics Trend. 2012 in late 2012 DeLorean was trading near 80, while the Japanese stock market, the Nick 2225 was languishing in the 8500 area. Japan was in a deep economic Funk, the country was on the wrong end of a multi-d decade, deflationary sucking machine. That had stopped all confidence and left an overvalued currency, and undervalued financial assets. That all changed with the announcement of ebonics. A major economic program spearheaded by prime minister Shinzo Abe. Ebonics. A series of initiatives that called for major structural reforms and massive monetary easing in Japan. Over the next 3 years, the nikay index rallied 250% and dollar Yen had an eye-popping Rally from 80 to 125. I know 3 traders that pretty much made their careers on that move. for whatever reason, I struggled to close my eyes and go with the move, positioning became extreme very quickly as 1, might imagine when a country's leader decides to devalue, the currency and ramp the equity Market higher I knew very well by that point in my career as I started in 1995 that when there's a major economic or policy shift positioning, doesn't matter. But for some reason, I had a mental block and struggled to go with the trend. I had seen enough times where positioning didn't matter for extended periods, so I should have known better. For example, in 2008, the global financial crisis. Most people were short stocks. Most of the way down 2000. 10 US quantitative easing, the market went short dollars and cleaned up and 2011, the Eurozone crisis the market was short Euro all the way down, though. Punchers did get badly rinsed. When euro dollar finally bought them, Eventually, positioning always matters but in the early and middle stages of watershed economic and policy changes, the macro is much bigger than any concern about positions. Thing is a dollar Yen climb from 80 to 90 to 100. I struggled massively to trade from the long side, and I was playing retracements and big levels and trying to top tick, 1 of the biggest economic stories of my lifetime. I still don't have a good sense of why I could not get myself to trade. The ebonics Trend successfully, I had various excuses, but no good understanding of where the mental block came from. But when a similar trade showed up in 2015, ECB quantitative easing, which drove your dollar from 1 140 to 105 in pretty much a straight line. I was ready I recognize the similarity of the setup and was strict about trading Euro only from the short side, till after the pair had already dropped massively lower. A hedge fund PM told me about how the founder of his fund and the firm's biggest risk. Taker put a Post-It note on his monitor in 2009 that said, long or flat. At that time, the authorities had just changed all the rules. By suspending Mark to Market, Banning short-selling, bailing out, the banks bailing out, the car companies, announcing quantitative easing at Etc and he realized it was going to be impossible for stocks to go down from that moment on I usually preach Nimmo as a key defining characteristic of successful short-term Traders. There is however, a time to have 1 cor View and stick to it. Identifying these rare moments where the markets will be 1 way for an extended period, can be the difference between an uninspired trading, career and a great 1. And mistake. Number 3 that I made Sprint. Ing out of the gates 1 recent December after a decent training year, I decided I was going to try something different in the new year. I'd been pretty consistent over the previous 5 or 6 years, putting up. Excellent, but not amazing, yearly p&l and I thought I've hit a plateau. I want to do something bigger, trade bigger, double last year's p&l. So instead of starting slowly and building a base of p&l before adding meaningful risk, I took a different approach. It just so happened that I had a very strong view that the dollar would sell off in the new year. So I decided to go all in right off the bat, and take a ton of risk on January 1. Take a guess. What happened? I got. Absolutely crushed. Losing half of my prior years, pnl. In the first 4 weeks. This put me in a devastating hole where I could barely trade for a while, as I scraped back and precariously avoided getting to the point where I would need to worry about my year to date. Stop loss sprinting out of the gates is a bad strategy. No matter how strong your view at the start of the year, there's too much path, dependence involved. If you go hard on day 1, even if you're placing what you think is an 80/20 bet. If that 20% comes up, you're so hobbled that you threaten your entire year. It's not worth the risk. You're essentially betting your entire year on a small sample. This is not good. I spent the next 6 months, scratching back to flat and managed to finish up a tiny bit on the air, but those 11 months were a grueling and painful Marathon the following year,
